T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | N O V E M B E R 2 0 2 6
President’s Message
by Don Gamble
Greetings from New Zealand!
I’ve been away for about a month, and I’m still here as I write
this. Of course I couldn’t resist looking up the local woodturners...
A Kiwi Guild night in Rotorua
Rotorua is famous for its geothermal activity. Steam rises
out of the ground all over town, and we visited several of the
thermal parks in the area, with their geysers, boiling mud
pools and hot springs. I’ll admit, though, that the highlight
of my stay was a Tuesday night with the Geyserland Guild of
Woodworkers.
Clement Le Lièvre (Clem), the Guild’s Secretary, set up my
visit and met me at their shed behind the Rotorua Museum,
a few blocks from the shore of Lake Rotorua. They have a
two-floor space of about 25 by 50 feet, with half a dozen
Nova lathes. People arrive right at 7:00pm. At 9:00pm the
lights go out and the night is over. What surprised me is that
they do this three or four times a week.
Their meetings aren’t like ours. Nobody is sitting in rows
watching a demo. Some people come to turn, and others
come for a coffee and a chat. Almost everyone there has a
lathe at home. They come to the shed to spend time with
other turners.
Clem wanted to send me home with some New Zealand
pen blanks. Paul overheard and said, “I have thousands at
my place. You got 20 minutes?” So off we went. Paul has
been in the wood business for more than 40 years and has
been turning for over 10. His house was a modest one-storey
home like many here, except there were logs, planks and
blanks everywhere. He has several lathes set up and more
stacked in a corner, and he still comes out to Guild nights.
That tells you what those evenings are about. He took me
to his pen blank room, which really did hold thousands of
blanks, and put together a collection of New Zealand woods
for me. Fingers crossed that Canadian border inspectors let
them through!
Then it was back to the shed for coffee, a cookie the treasurer had baked, and a lot of woodturning talk. It was a great
group and a very different way to run a Guild.
New KMS Abbotsford Studio
A huge thank you to Bill Fowle, Brian Lunt and Ed Pretty for
keeping things moving while I’ve been away. The lease is
signed. The breakdown of our Coquitlam shop is essentially
done, thanks to Brian for coordinating it. The electrical work
should be finished by early December. Through December
and January we’ll be setting up the new space: installing the
lathes, bandsaw and air filters, and mounting the accessories on the walls. If you’d like to lend a hand, please get in
touch with Brian.
The new studio will be a home for visiting demonstrators,
Guild classes and drop-in sessions. Having seen how the
drop-in model works in New Zealand, I’m keen to look at
what we could do with it.
We’ve also been talking with the Fraser Valley Woodturners
Guild about the studio, and we’ll keep working with them on
ways to include them. A bigger woodturning community is
good for all of us.
I’m looking forward to getting home, turning a few things
alongside all of you, and enjoying a coffee and someone’s
home baking, New Zealand style.

Editor’s Notes
by Britchie
Just a brief note from me this month to express my gratitude to several of our members who have stepped-up with
content for this issue.
Firstly, a big thank you to Chris Stiles, who not only gave us
an excellent live presentation at Sapperton Hall last month
on how to make his signature three-pointed boxes, but also
agreed to write-up a cover story describing how he prepared
for that. If that were not enough, you’ll also find a short article from him on his experience with making and using his
own Captive Ring Tool in the “Tools, Tech & Tips” section.
Thanks also to our past President, Steve Hansen for putting
together a detailed and well illustrated article on the options
for holding vessels securely for finishing-off the foot details.
And lastly but not leastly, my main man, Brian Lunt who on
top of everything else he’s been invlolved with this month,
found the time to get photos of both the Fall 2026 Intro to
Spindle Turning Class run by Ed Pretty and the work being
done to transition our lathe turning classroom to a new location in Abbotsford. The work being undertaken by volunteers is significant and I trust the photos will give everyone
some insight into this exciting development for our Guild.
See the photo galleries toward the end of this issue for this
and other recent events.
Happy turning.

15% Discount for GVWG Members
If you give the cashier your phone number, you will only get
the store 5% non-Guild discount. By saying GVWG instead you
get the 15% Guild discount.
If you are buying something that needs a warranty, just give
them your Name and Address and that will go on the electronic file. If the item you are buying has a flyer sale that is better
than the 15%, then you will automatically get the better rate.
Every purchase you make in the store by using this process
adds to our GVWG Credit account which we use to buy KMS
gift certificate prizes. We even bought our Laguna lathe for
Sapperton Hall with this! By doing this you are giving yourself
a better discount and helping the guild at the same time.
If you are an out-of-town Guild member, all you have to do is
type in GVWG as the customer name when buying, and type in
your full name, address etc. in the ‘ship-to’ field and you will
get the 15% discount.
The 15% is an average savings and is based on the cost margins from that manufacturer. This does not apply to published
special flyer items. If we all do this, we can even get up to a
bigger discount level in future!

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | N O V E M B E R 2 0 2 6
Practice makes
Perfect
by Chris Stiles
The first time I saw three pointed boxes was during a demo
I attended in Ottawa. It was several years between that and
when I finally decided to try it for myself. I was probably
desperate for a fresh gift idea for my nieces and I may have
seen an article in American Woodturner that reminded me.
I made a couple and then forgot about them until recently
when I was asked to demonstrate for the Guild. I knew I
wasn’t prepared for this right away but it seemed doable
with a bit of practice. I tried to postpone it as long as possible but someone had already taken the November spot!
Finding some wood to practice with, I went to my workshop to get going on it. The first piece never made it out
of the workshop. At some point it came out of the chuck
and shattered beyond repair. The second piece I completed successfully but only after about five hours of shop
time and a few glue repairs—which I conveniently do not
remember in detail.
At this point I began wondering what I had gotten myself
into. Maybe it was going to be too much for one night and I
would have to stage things with a few partially done pieces
that I could pull out at different steps. Or maybe I should
only demonstrate some of it and leave the rest for people
to figure out. In any case, I was going to have turn some
more to figure out those details so I found myself some
more wood and went back at it.
The next practice piece took a couple of hours less. The
one after, I tried some spalted wood and miscalculated
the thickness of the wings, so it became a box without the
corners. I noticed each time I got a little bit faster and a
little bit better. I began putting a timer on while I practiced
the steps I planned to show during the demo. And since I
was not going to be sanding, it meant that I could skip finishing the bottom of the box or the lid which saved a bit of
time. As the demo crept closer I noticed I was well within a
reasonable timeframe but I knew it would take a bit longer
in front of people with them talking, answering questions
and so on.
As a final bit of practice, I arm-twisted a few people into
watching me practice on the Saturday before the demo.
That went well and I decided to trust in this and the muscle
memory I had developed and in the final days before the
demo all I did was gather my tools and make sure everything was sharp.
In the end I completed seven practice pieces. I had one
piece that didn’t survive and a couple more to complete
from the practice demos and the live demo. There is
nothing quite like repetitive turning to sharpen your skills.
And having to explain it to an audience makes you to think
things through more deliberately and leads to a deeper
understanding for yourself as well. So if you really want to
get better at something—volunteer, or say ‘Yes’ the next
time you are asked to demonstrate.

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | N O V E M B E R 2 0 2 6
Dale Larson is widely regarded as one of the most accomplished and influential woodturners working today and his visit is a rare opportunity for our members and the wider turning
community to learn directly from a true master of the craft.
Dale lives in Gresham, Oregon, and has been turning wood for
nearly five decades. He bought his first lathe, a half-horsepower Craftsman from a Sears catalogue, in 1978, and began selling his bowls through galleries in 1991. His specialty is Pacific
Madrone, bigleaf Maple, English and black Walnut, and some
Cherry. To work with the notoriously difficult Pacific Madrone,
he boils roughed-out blanks in a large stainless-steel, firewood
heated tank for two hours and then air-dries them, a technique
that reflects both his practical farmboy roots and his deep
knowledge of wood behaviour. His 30’ x 44’ shop, rebuilt in
2014 holds 600 to 800 roughed-out bowls, of which he finishes
200 to 225 in a year, plus about fifteen ovals and many spheres.
His bowls are currently sold through seven galleries across the
United States.
Dale’s teaching and demonstration resume is equally impressive. He has demonstrated at five AAW Symposiums, eight

Dale Larson
visit in Feb 2027
by Don Gamble
We are delighted to welcome Dale Larson,
renowned bowl turner, respected educator
and 2019 AAW Honorary Lifetime Member,
for a special 3-day visit in February 2027.
(Continues on the next page)

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | N O V E M B E R 2 0 2 6
818
regional symposia, and numerous local chapters, as well as
international events in England and Israel. Regional symposia have included stops in Rocky Mountain, Vancouver BC,
Utah, Tennessee, Georgia, Florida, and Oregon. He has taught
woodturning classes at the John C. Campbell Folk School and
Arrowmont School of Arts and Crafts. His demonstrations are
known for their clarity, practicality and generosity: he shares
not only techniques, but the reasoning and experience behind
them. He has also written articles about wood and woodturning published in American Woodturner, World of Wood, Woodworker West, Woodturning Design, and L’echo des Copeaux
(AFTAB France).
Dale has given a great deal back to the craft. He is a founding
member and twice-past president of the Cascade Woodturners in Portland, Oregon. He served on the AAW Board from
2009 to 2014, three years as President, and received the 2019
Honorary Lifetime Member award for his technical mastery
and decades of service.
Before woodturning became the centre of his life, Dale spent
thirty years in law enforcement, retiring from the Portland area
in 2004. That background (methodical, direct and focused
on getting things right) is evident in everything from his shop
management philosophy to his approach to teaching.
What sets Dale apart is his philosophy of woodturning as a
living, ancient tradition. In his own words: “Woodturning has
been practiced for five to seven thousand years, and I see
myself as one small continuation of a very long tradition.” He
is equally grounded about the work itself: “I have been turning
for forty years now and my bowls are still getting better. I am
still learning.” Whether discussing moisture content, tool
control, or the subtleties of form, Dale brings a depth of insight
that resonates with beginners and experienced turners alike.
Notably, Dale has demonstrated in Vancouver BC before, so he
knows our regional woodturning community. We are honoured to welcome him back and to host him for what promises
to be one of the most inspiring and educational weekends of
our 2027 program. Mark your calendars for February 20 to 22,
2027.
Details and registration links for the demo and workshops are
on our web site: https://www.gvwg.ca

M E M B E R A R T I C L E
There are four ways to hold your work for that final phase: vacuum chucking, between centres, donuts, and pinching (with a
little flower arranging).
FIG. 1
Vacuum chucking (fig.1) provides perfect access to work the
foot. It requires specialized equipment and a good understanding of air pressure. I possess neither, so I leave this
method to others.
FIG. 2
Driving between centres (fig.2) is easy and provides excellent
alignment and reasonable support so long as your cuts are
very light. It has a drawback in that you can never completely
cleanup up the foot because your drive centre gets in the way.
Final cleanup must be done off the lathe.
FIG. 3
The donut chucking method (fig.3) uses a hoop (the donut) to
sandwich the form’s body against a plate or cylinder. Like the
vacuum chuck its advantage is that you do not have a pesky
tail stock in the way and are free to turn and sand everything
as you will. It does require you to make your own chuck but
this is very doable and inexpensive.
Flower arranging
meets wood turning
by Steve Hansen
I like making hollow forms with small or
natural edge openings. Just like making
bowls there are three phases to completion:
shape the exterior, excavate the interior,
and finish off the foot. The finishing of the
foot is the focus of this article.
(Continues on the next page)

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | N O V E M B E R 2 0 2 6
8
M E M B E R A R T I C L E
FIG. 4
The pinching method (fig.4) is employed when you have a very
delicate form which might collapse if held between centres. Or
perhaps it has a wane edge which renders centre work useless.
To create the pinch, a mandrel driven from the headstock
provides reach to the interior bottom of your form and allows
tail stock pressure to pinch against the mandrel. Traditionally
the mandrel is faced on its end with a pad of sand paper which
provides the ‘bite’ on the wood. The pinch requires a very light
touch while turning.
What about flower arrangement? Many years ago while employing the pinch method, I encountered a problem while cutting: the wood stopped revolving while the mandrel remained
spinning inside… abrading a hole inside and within a moment
the piece let go of its grip – damage ensued. Now what!?!
Around about this time, I remembered scratching myself on
a Japanese flower frog, also known as “kenzan”. These things
typically have dozens of closely packed needles. I wondered,
could this multi-pronged thing provide an alternative to the
sand paper grip? I examined one and stuck it into a few different boards and determined that unlike sand paper, it stuck
in place very well with minimal pressure. So, I drilled a hole
through the centre; replaced the sand paper with the kenzan. I
re-mounted the piece and it drove perfectly without slip. Surprisingly, after turning, the kenzan needles left hardly a trace.
I have since made a few of these grippers from scratch. The
photo (bottom-left) shows three examples including a kenzan,
a modified kenzan with bolt, and a homemade needle gripper
made from a knurled bolt. The innovation allows me more
confidence and flexibility when completing tricky hollow
forms.

YOUR PERSONAL SAFETY
Always wear Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) such as
approved safety glasses or goggles that include side protectors. Use a full face shield for larger bowl, vessel, or any turning
involving chucks and faceplates. Wear a dust mask or an air
filtration helmet in conjunction with proper ventilation and/
or a dust collection system as appropriate. Remember—it’s
the fine airborne particles that are harmful to your respiratory
system. Wear hearing protection during extended periods of
turning.
Tie back long hair and avoid long sleeves or loose clothing.
Remove rings and other jewelry, or any dangling objects that
may catch on rotating parts or accessories.
Stay alert. Watch what you are doing. Pay close attention to
unusual sounds or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the
cause. Don’t operate machines when you are tired or under
the influence of drugs or alcohol.
WORKING SAFELY WITH YOUR LATHE
Ensure your workpiece is securely fastened. When using a
faceplate, be certain the workpiece is solidly mounted with
stout screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws as a minimum).
Do not use drywall or deck screws. When turning between
centers, check the workpiece is firmly mounted between the
headstock and tailstock and rotate your workpiece forwards/
backwards by hand to make sure it clears the toolrest and bed
before turning the lathe on.
Check all locking devices on the tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest and base) are tight before operating the lathe.
Check the speed of your lathe BEFORE turning it on. Use
slower speeds for larger diameters or rough pieces and higher
speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced.
Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is
balanced. If the lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the speed.
If the workpiece vibrates, always stop the machine to understand why. As a starting point, consult your operator’s manual
for recommended speeds for a particular lathe. Ensure the
lathe speed is compatible with the diameter of the blank.
Stay clear of danger zones directly behind and in front of the
workpiece. They are the most likely areas for a piece to travel
as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of
this zone when turning on the lathe, keeping your hand on the
switch in case you need to turn the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
Turn the lathe off before adjusting anything including the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
Always remove chuck keys, adjusting wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in place,
even for a moment. Always remove the tool rest before sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
Know your capabilities and limitations. An experienced
woodturner is capable of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning turners.
Exercise extra caution when using stock with cracks, splits,
checks, bark pockets, knots, irregular shapes or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types of stock until they have
greater knowledge of working such wood.
Hold turning tools securely on the toolrest, holding the tool
in a controlled but comfortable manner. Always contact the
tool rest with the tool before contacting the wood.
Never work with a lathe in reverse unless the chuck is using
a locking set-screw. It is possible for a chuck or faceplate to
unscrew unless it is fitted securely on the lathe spindle.
Don’t overreach. Keep proper footing and keep your balance

S A F E T Y G U I D E L I N E S
(Continues on the next page)
You mostly work on your own so safety is
YOUR responsibility. Please take the time to
read our safety guidelines and make them part
of your daily turning practice. Be safe out there!

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | N O V E M B E R 2 0 2 6
at all times.
Keep tools sharp and clean for better and safer performance.
Don’t force a dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose for which
it was not designed or intended.
Consider your work environment. Don’t use a lathe in damp
or wet locations. Do not use in presence of flammable liquids
or gases, and always keep a fully-charged fire extinguisher
close at hand. Keep your work area well lit.
Guard against electric shock. Inspect electric cords for damage. Avoid the use of extension cords.
Never leave a lathe running unattended. Turn power off.
Don’t leave lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
SAFETY MAINTENANCE
Keep your lathe in good repair. Ensure belt guards or protective covers are in place. Check for damaged parts, alignment,
binding of moving parts, and other conditions that may affect
its operation.
Read and follow safety guidelines for your lathe and other
workshop equipment. Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially bandsaws and chainsaws.

Getting all the Paint out of
Rattle Cans
by Brian Lunt
How do you get the remaining paint out of a Rattle Can when it
has run out of pressure?
Answer: attach a flexible hose and re-pressurize it.
Using a tubeless tire valve, rock it back and forth to get it to
grip over the top of the can’s exit port. Attach a flexible hose to
this and pump-in some air to the required pressure.
The pressure inside a typical
aerosol spray can is usually between 60 to 100 psi. This is necessary for the can to effectively
dispense its contents when the
nozzle is activated.
Maintaining the correct
pressure ensures the contents
are atomized properly for an

Stopping Wood Glue Blocks
Moving While Clamping
by Brian Lunt
I recently had to glue up 35 glue blocks to pre-cut shallow
bowl blanks after we had to cancel the Matt Monaco classes.
One problem I usually experienced, was the two glued pieces
“skating” when applying pressure with clamps and losing centre position. Remembering a technique I heard of and checking on how to do it, I proceeded with fantastic success.
The key point worth emphasizing: the salt is not part of the
glue joint – it is only a temporary traction point to prevent the
pieces from skating while clamping. We are talking very few
grains of salt being used. Like 12 grains. The fewer the better. If
you sprinkle salt on your work like they were French fries, you
will compromise your glue and create an unsafe joint. Salt is
a better choice than sand in my opinion as sand will dull the
edge of a gouge.

Safety Considerations
When working with aerosol cans: Always wear safety glasses
to protect your eyes from potential spray. Be cautious of the
pressure, as exceeding the recommended levels can lead to
malfunction or even explosion.

Captive Ring Tool
by Chris Stiles
When I first decided to try making captive rings I did not feel
like spending the money to purchase a ring tool. Instead I
picked up a screwdriver from the local dollar store and ground
into a shape I thought would work. It worked so well that I
never actually felt the need to go out and spend money on a
ring tool.
Recently I had a student who very much wanted to learn how
to make a wedding goblet. Her son was getting married in the
Fall and she wanted to make a goblet for the occasion. While
I was willing to teach her there was a problem since many of
my tools were in storage to prepare for a move. I explained
the situation and told her it would have to wait until after the
move when I could reach my tools.
One of the next times I saw her she pulled out ring tool that
she had purchased and when I mentioned to her that I had
never actually used one like that she offered to lend it to me

eventually figured out how to use the ring tool and gave her

She now has a wedding goblet for her son and knows how to
use the ring tool. In the end though I still wound up preferring
the screwdriver I first ground into a ring tool years ago. Perhaps it just a matter of practice but I find I can cut the underside of the rings more cleanly with my screwdriver tool than
with the tool designed for it.
